title: Two Equal Cells, and One Wins

scenes.tts: In the fly embryo, the cells that will make the nervous system sit in small groups. The cells start out equal, and every cell can become a neural precursor. Yet usually only one does. Something must break the tie. First the group becomes able, and then the cells signal to each other until one wins.
scenes.visual: A cluster of five equal cells; all turn green-rimmed, then one is chosen and the rest dim; a question mark appears.
scenes.narration: In the fly embryo, the cells that will make the nervous system sit in small groups. The cells start out equal, and every cell can become a neural precursor. Yet usually only one does. Something must break the tie. First the group becomes able, and then the cells signal to each other until one wins.

scenes.tts: Take two neighbours in the cluster. Proneural genes encode transcription factors that make both cells able to become neural. Think of it as a casting call, where everyone gets to audition. Proneural proteins raise their own expression, and in the textbook model they also raise Delta. Delta is a protein in the cell membrane.
scenes.visual: Two of the cells grow into a large pair; green proneural bars rise with a self-activation loop; yellow Delta knobs grow on the membranes.
scenes.narration: Take two neighbours in the cluster. Proneural genes encode transcription factors that make both cells able to become neural. Think of it as a casting call, where everyone gets to audition. Proneural proteins raise their own expression, and in the textbook model they also raise Delta. Delta is a protein in the cell membrane.

scenes.tts: Delta on one cell binds Notch on the cell it touches, and pulls. Two cuts then free the inner part of Notch. That part enters the nucleus. There, with a protein called C S L, it turns on the Enhancer of split genes. These genes encode repressors that switch proneural genes off.

scenes.visual: Cell A's Delta knob slides into cell B's blue Notch cup; a blue piece enters B's nucleus, a red repressor bar rises and the green proneural bar falls.
scenes.narration: Delta on one cell binds Notch on the cell it touches, and pulls. Two cuts then free the inner part of Notch. That part enters the nucleus. There, with a protein called CSL, it turns on the Enhancer of split genes. These genes encode repressors that switch proneural genes off.

scenes.tts: Follow the loop. More Delta on cell A means more Notch activity in cell B. Cell B makes more repressor, so it has less proneural activity and less Delta. Then cell A gets less Notch activity, and its proneural activity rises. The loop has closed, and cell A has pulled ahead.
scenes.visual: Both cells reset to balance; the loop is stepped through, one bar or knob changing per phrase, ending with A high and B low.
scenes.narration: Follow the loop. More Delta on cell A means more Notch activity in cell B. Cell B makes more repressor, so it has less proneural activity and less Delta. Then cell A gets less Notch activity, and its proneural activity rises. The loop has closed, and cell A has pulled ahead.

scenes.tts: Each cell inhibits its neighbour, so two inhibitions in a row make positive feedback. A perfectly balanced pair could sit in the middle, like a pencil on its point. But noise gives one cell slightly more Delta. The loop magnifies that small difference until one cell becomes the neural precursor. Either outcome is stable, and which cell wins is a matter of chance.
scenes.visual: Balanced bars, a tiny nudge to cell A's Delta, then the simulated loop drives A up and B down; A is marked the neural precursor.
scenes.narration: Each cell inhibits its neighbour, so two inhibitions in a row make positive feedback. A perfectly balanced pair could sit in the middle, like a pencil on its point. But noise gives one cell slightly more Delta. The loop magnifies that small difference until one cell becomes the neural precursor. Either outcome is stable, and which cell wins is a matter of chance.

scenes.tts: Now take Notch away from the embryo. Without the receptor, no cell can be told, not you. Both cells keep their proneural genes on, and both become neural. In the whole embryo, that means far too many neuroblasts and too little skin. What decides a cell's fate is how its signaling compares with that of the cells beside it.
scenes.visual: Notch and the inhibition arrows are removed; both proneural bars stay high and both cells turn green; then the working loop returns and a compare arrow joins the two cells.
